units.text: Information notice on the application of CBAM following incorporation of CBAM in the EEA Agreement

This notice is intended to facilitate the uniform application of Regulation (EU) 2023/956 establishing a carbon border adjustment mechanism (“the CBAM Regulation”) in the European Economic Area (“EEA”) and to clarify the treatment of goods, imported from, or moved between the European Union and the EEA EFTA States to all concerned stakeholders. This notice is without prejudice to the binding interpretation of Union law, the EEA Agreement and the relevant decisions of the EEA Joint Committee, as well as the jurisdiction of the Court of Justice of the European Union and the EFTA Court within their respective competences.

Decision 283/2026 of the EEA Joint Committee, adopted on 25 September 2026, incorporates 1 Regulation and its amending Regulation into the EEA Agreement￼. In doing so, it extends the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) to Iceland and Norway, thereby creating a common CBAM area. The Decision is not applicable to Liechtenstein.

The technical and financial arrangements for the participation of Iceland and Norway in the CBAM Registry and the common central platform are instead covered by Decision 287/2026 of the EEA Joint Committee.

Norway and Iceland will apply the CBAM fully as of 1 January 2027. As Norway and Iceland will no longer be considered third countries for CBAM purposes, they will be deleted from Annex III of the CBAM Regulation. Importers established in Norway or Iceland will no longer need to use an indirect customs representative for CBAM purposes when importing CBAM goods into the EU, and vice versa. However, they will still have to use customs representation for the purpose of the application of the Union Customs Code. Decision 283/2026 entered into force on 18 November 2026. As of this date, economic operators established in Norway or Iceland can apply for CBAM authorisations with their national competent authority.
1. Single mass-based threshold of 50 tonnes (de minimis exemption)

As of 1 January 2027, the annual cumulative threshold of 50 tonnes applicable to imports of aluminium, iron and steel, fertilisers, and cement, pursuant to Article 2a of the CBAM Regulation, will apply jointly to importations into the Union and the customs territories of Norway and Iceland.

Economic operators exceeding such threshold, or importing any quantity of electricity and hydrogen, will have to hold a CBAM authorisation. EU-established economic operators conducting businesses in Norway and Iceland should therefore consider all imports in the three customs territories collectively as concerns compliance with the annual cumulative threshold.
2. Identification of economic operators
For goods declared to customs, economic operators must continue to use the trader identification number required in the country of import:
• in the EU, the EORI number is used;
• in Norway, the Norwegian organisation number/TIN (Organisasjonsnummer) is used;
• in Iceland, the Icelandic national identification number/TIN (Kennitalais) is used.
3. Mutual recognition of CBAM authorisations
Economic operators established in Norway or Iceland must submit their CBAM applications before importing CBAM goods and latest by 31 March 2027, by following these steps:
• register for access to Uniform User Management & Digital Signatures (UUM&DS) by
contacting your national competent authority (contact details are available here).
• obtain a UUM&DS profile to access the Authorisation Management Module (AMM)
of the CBAM Registry from your national competent authority.
• launch and submit the application in the AMM, at this link.

A mutual recognition of CBAM authorisations, issued under Articles 5 and 17 of the CBAM Regulation, applies. This means that an importer established in the EU will be able to use the CBAM authorisation issued in the EU to import into Norway or Iceland, and vice versa.

The identification numbers used must however be linked. For the checks of CBAM authorisations to be possible, economic operators that have been assigned a corporate identifier used in another country must inform the relevant competent authority accordingly. This is foreseen in adaptations to Article 5 of the CBAM Regulation under Joint Committee Decision 283/2026.
4. TCUIN in the EORI record

Particular attention must be paid to data element 8 “Third Country Unique Identification Number” (TCUIN) provided for in Annex 12-01 to Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/2446. Although the collection of this data element is optional for EU Member States under the general EORI rules, it is required for economic operators established in Norway or Iceland to declare CBAM goods to EU customs. The TCUIN should contain the relevant Norwegian or Icelandic national trader identification number. This allows the EORI number used in the EU to be linked to the national identifier used for the same operator in Norway or Iceland.

From 1 January 2027, EORI-registered economic operators established in Norway or Iceland that are involved in CBAM operations must use the TCUIN when declaring goods to EU customs. Failure to match the TCUIN of an economic operator with its EORI number may result in rejection of imports into the EU, in Norway or in Iceland.
5. What economic operators need to do as regards TCUIN and EORI
Economic operators established in Norway or Iceland that intend to import CBAM goods into the EU should:
• ensure that they have an EORI number assigned by an EU Member State;
• provide their Norwegian or Icelandic national trader identification number as TCUIN when requesting an EORI number;
• check that their Norwegian or Icelandic national trader identification number is correctly recorded as TCUIN in their EORI record;
• contact the EU customs authority responsible for their EORI registration to update the record if data element 8 (“TCUIN”) is missing or incorrect.

The EORI number does not replace the national identifier used in customs declarations in Norway or Iceland. Moreover, economic operators that only import in Norway or Iceland are not required to obtain an EORI number. Likewise, economic operators established in the customs territory of the Union are not required to obtain a Norwegian or Icelandic TIN number unless they intend to declare goods to customs in those countries.
6. What customs administrations need to do as regards TCUIN and EORI
For economic operators established in Norway and Iceland and carrying out customs operations involving CBAM goods in the EU, customs authorities of EU Member States should:
• register the economic operator in the EOS/EORI electronic system when it requests an EORI number to carry out such customs operations and the conditions for EORI registration are met;
• ask the operator to provide its Norwegian or Icelandic national trader identification number and record this number in data element 8 (“TCUIN”) in the EORI record;
• check the TCUIN before recording it to ensure that it belongs to the same economic operator being registered in EORI;
• for economic operators already registered in the EOS/EORI electronic system, check that the TCUIN is recorded and correct and complete or correct the EORI record where needed;
• update the EORI record when the national trader identifier number changes or incorrect information is identified.
7. Regime for third country goods previously released for free circulation in the Union or EEA EFTA States, Norway or Iceland (and conversely)

As of 1 January 2027, CBAM goods originating in third countries other than those listed in Annex III to the CBAM Regulation, that have already been released for free circulation in either the EU or Norway or Iceland and have already been subject to CBAM on that occasion, will be exempted from CBAM if they are subsequently released for free circulation in the EU and vice versa. The customs declarant will have to indicate in the subsequent customs declaration lodged in the customs territory of the Union that the goods have been previously released for free circulation in the customs territory of any of the above-mentioned EEA EFTA States.

TARIC code Y423 will be used for goods that have already been released for free circulation within the customs territory of Norway or Iceland (from 1 January 2027) and will be used for imports to the EU. A similar code should apply in Norway and Iceland to signal that CBAM goods have been previously released for free circulation in the EU or in Norway/Iceland.

The declarant will have to make available documentation or information proving that the goods have been previously released for free circulation within the customs territory of the respective EFTA States. The customs declarant will also bear responsibility for the availability of this proof at the time of lodging of the customs declaration.

In line with the provisions of the CBAM Regulation, operators applying for authorisation in Norway and Iceland will also benefit from an exemption until 31 March of the first year of CBAM’s implementation. Importers established in Norway or Iceland that submit an application by 31 March 2027 may indeed continue importing goods until the relevant competent authority has taken a decision on their application. They will not be required to hold a CBAM authorisation before importing CBAM goods, which will instead be mandatory from 31 March 2027 onwards.
8. Regime for processed products resulting from the inward processing procedure and re-exported to Norway or Iceland (and conversely re-exported to the Union)

CBAM obligations will apply to processed products from goods listed in Annex I originating in a third country that are resulting from the inward processing procedure referred to in Article 256 of Regulation (EU) No 952/2013, where they are re-exported to the customs territory of Norway or Iceland, provided that they are imported in one of those customs territories.

The Commission’s proposal amending the CBAM Regulation as regards the extension of its scope to downstream goods and anti-circumvention measures provides for the conferral of implementing powers on the Commission in this regard. Once the amending Regulation has been adopted, the Commission will be empowered to adopt the relevant implementing act rules, in accordance with the procedures laid down therein.
